notes: PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — check_transaction was not read-only. It calls check_and_authorize, which adds value to spent_wei and (since the persistence work) writes that to disk. Used as a pre-flight it charged the hard cap twice per transfer, and any value above half the remaining headroom tripped the auto kill switch with no ETH moved. Fixed by adding a genuinely read-only sibling rather than changing the existing call.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — one guard implementation, not two. Extracted EnvelopeEngine::evaluate(env, request, now) -> Result<(), EnvelopeError>: a pure function holding every rule (kill switch, expiry, empty scope, out of scope, per-tx ceiling, hard-cap headroom) in that order. check_and_authorize now calls it and only adds the side effects (audit entry, auto kill switch, spend accounting, persist); preview calls it and adds nothing. Divergence is impossible by construction, and a case-table test asserts the two verdicts match across 10 scenarios including the boundary cases (exactly at the cap, exactly at the ceiling, zero value) and the precedence case (kill switch outranks an out-of-scope address).

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — check_and_authorize's behaviour, signature and audit output are unchanged. The audit-event mapping (KillSwitchBlocked/'kill_switch', EnvelopeExpired/'expired', ScopeViolation/'out_of_scope', PerTxCeilingViolation/'per_tx_ceiling', HardCapViolation/'hard_cap' + KillSwitchActivated, and NoScopeDefined deliberately not audited) was preserved case for case, as was the auto-kill-switch-then-persist ordering. All 6 pre-existing engine tests still pass untouched.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — new Tauri command preview_transaction(to, value_wei, calldata?) -> TransactionPreview, and control-server route POST /preview-transaction with the same body. value_wei is a DECIMAL STRING, not an f64 of ETH: wei does not survive a JS number, and a pre-flight check that silently re-rounds the amount it is checking is not a check. (check_transaction keeps its f64 value_eth parameter — unchanged, as instructed.)

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — TransactionPreview returns: authorized, reject_code (stable codes no_envelope|kill_switch|expired|no_scope|out_of_scope|per_tx_ceiling|hard_cap), reject_reason (a sentence to show the user), reject_detail (the Debug form check_transaction already returns, so existing error handling keeps working), envelope_active, kill_switch, expires_at, in_scope, and value_wei / per_tx_ceiling_wei / hard_cap_wei / spent_wei / remaining_wei as decimal strings. in_scope is reported independently of authorized so a UI can flag a bad destination even when the kill switch is what actually refused.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — get_envelope_status now includes per_tx_ceiling_wei (additive field, u128-as-string like its siblings). It was genuinely absent, which is why the frontend could not check the ceiling at all.
PM ROUND 2, ITEM 1 — check_transaction's doc comment now states in the first line that it consumes budget, what the double-charge and kill-switch consequences are, and points at preview_transaction.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — nonce reuse. sign_and_send read the nonce with eth_getTransactionCount(..., 'latest'), so two sends before the first was mined got the same nonce and the second REPLACED the first — two hashes shown, one transfer silently gone. Fixed with three things together, because none alone is sufficient: (a) 'pending' instead of 'latest', since 'latest' cannot see the mempool; (b) a per-from-address tokio Mutex held across read-nonce -> sign -> broadcast, since 'pending' alone is still racy under concurrency; (c) an in-process record of the last nonce used, since even a serialised second read can come back stale before the node has counted our broadcast.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — the allocation rule is max(cached_next, chain_pending): trust our own record when the node is behind, trust the node when it is ahead (the same key used from another wallet client, or after a restart when there is no record). A test drives a deliberately flapping node value and asserts the allocated nonce never goes backwards.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — the record advances ONLY on a confirmed broadcast (commit). Any failed send invalidates it, not just nonce faults: a transport error or timeout can hide a transaction that did reach the mempool, and re-reading 'pending' is always the safe direction.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — 'nonce too low', 'replacement transaction underpriced' / 'replacement fee too low' and 'already known' are classified explicitly (case-insensitive substring, since no node exposes a stable code for these). On any of them the chain is re-read and a clear error is returned. The replacement message says outright that another transaction with that nonce is pending, that sending would have REPLACED it, and that Westron refused rather than cancel a transfer the user did not ask to cancel. Unrelated failures (insufficient funds, intrinsic gas too low, base-fee errors, HTTP errors) are asserted NOT to be misclassified.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — nonce slots are keyed case-insensitively. An EIP-55 checksummed address and its lowercase spelling are one account; treating them as two slots would hand out the same nonce twice and reintroduce the exact bug. There is a test for it.

PM ROUND 2, ITEM 2 — tests use a fake nonce source and never touch the network. The headline one runs 25 concurrent tokio tasks sending from one address against a node value that never updates (the worst case, and the one that produced the original bug), holding the real lock across a real await point, and asserts all 25 nonces are distinct and contiguous.

PM ROUND 2 — FOR THE FRONTEND (1/2): preview_transaction now exists, so the zero-value-pre-flight workaround in WalletDetailClient.tsx can be replaced. Call preview_transaction { to, value_wei: <decimal wei string>, calldata: null } with the REAL amount. It spends nothing, persists nothing and writes no audit entry, so it is safe to call on every keystroke. It returns authorized plus reject_code / reject_reason and all four wei limits as strings, so the manual BigInt hard-cap re-check can go too — including the per-tx ceiling, which you could not check before because get_envelope_status did not expose it (it does now). Keep calling the existing consuming path exactly once at send time; nothing about it changed.

PM ROUND 2 — FOR THE FRONTEND (2/2): the multi-destination block can be lifted. Sends from one address are now serialised in-process and nonces increment across them, so N transfers from one wallet get N distinct nonces whether issued sequentially or concurrently. Two caveats worth surfacing in the UI rather than hiding: sends from one address are now strictly sequential, so N transfers take N round-trips and a progress indicator is more honest than a spinner; and if a transfer fails mid-batch the remaining ones still need the user's decision, since each one separately consumes envelope budget. Every destination must be in the envelope scope.

ITEM 1 — Keychain. wallet/keychain.rs no longer writes plaintext private keys. On macOS every secret is a generic-password Keychain item, service "Westron", account = the existing key name (wallet_<address>, alchemy, opensea, etherscan). All eight public function signatures are unchanged, so no caller moved. normalize_api_key is still applied on both read and write for the three API keys.

ITEM 1 — non-macOS fallback. Other platforms keep a file backend so the crate builds and tests everywhere, but a key file is now created via OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).mode(0o600) and renamed into place — never fs::write-then-chmod. There is no instant at which the file exists world-readable. A unix test asserts mode 0600 immediately after creation, and again after an overwrite.

ITEM 1 — migration ordering. For each existing *.key file: read, write to the Keychain, read back, compare, and ONLY on an exact match unlink the plaintext. Any failure (store failed, read-back failed, read-back mismatched, or unlink failed) leaves the file where it is and counts it as `pending`. Four separate tests pin 'a key that was not confirmed elsewhere is never deleted'. Empty key files are skipped rather than treated as failures. The sweep runs once per process, behind a OnceLock, from every public entry point.

ITEM 1 — logging. Migration logs counts only ('N key(s) moved into the macOS Keychain, M left on disk') plus an error line naming the failing entry. No key material and no file contents are ever logged.

ITEM 1 — status surface. keychain_status() -> {backend: "keychain"|"file", migrated, pending, last_error}. Exposed on GET /status as the `keychain` object and via exactly one new Tauri command, get_keychain_status (the only addition to the invoke_handler list). pending > 0 is the signal that a plaintext private key is still on disk and needs a human.

ITEM 1 — dependency. security-framework = "3" added under [target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies], so Linux builds do not pull it in. Cargo.lock already contained security-framework 3.7.0 as a transitive dependency, so the lock diff is a single line and no new crate version enters the build.

ITEM 2 — new src-tauri/src/persist.rs. Small JSON state store: app_file(name), write_json/read_json, and write_private_atomic (temp file created 0600, then renamed). A missing file reads as None; a CORRUPT file is an error, never a silent reset — the caller decides how to fail, and both callers fail closed.

ITEM 2 — envelope. EnvelopeEngine gained an optional store. new() stays memory-only so existing tests (and any future embedded use) cannot stomp on the real user's file; load_or_new() is what lib.rs::run() uses. Persistence happens at every mutation: create, authorize (spend), auto kill switch on a hard-cap breach, manual kill switch on/off, revoke. spent_wei is written before check_and_authorize returns Ok, so a crash between the check and the next write cannot hand the hard cap back.

ITEM 2 — envelope restore rules. An envelope whose expires_at has passed is NOT restored as active and the file is normalised on load. Everything else comes back verbatim including spent_wei and kill_switch_active. Unreadable state restores nothing — 'no authorisation', never 'no limits'. Tests: round-trip, spent_wei preserved (with a follow-on hard-cap breach to prove the counter is real, not cosmetic), expired-not-restored, kill-switch-stays-on (and its release also persists, or the user could never recover), auto-kill-switch persisted, revoke clears, memory-only writes nothing.

ITEM 2 — scheduler. SchedulerHandle gained the same optional store; control::start now uses load_or_new(false). The 'ships disabled' product decision is untouched — it is now the FIRST-LAUNCH default rather than a reset on every restart. Only enabled + interval_secs persist; cycles_run / last_check_at / last_cycle are per-run and deliberately not restored, so a freshly started loop cannot misreport having just checked something. A corrupt state file falls back to disabled, never to armed. Persisted intervals are re-clamped on load.

ITEM 3 — the STATUS.md hypothesis is wrong and was NOT implemented. The key stays out of the URL path; client.rs's prices_v1_base() + bearer_auth are unchanged. This is now written down in the price_poller module docs, in the two advice strings, and in the probe script, with two tests asserting the advice text still says 'Authorization: Bearer' and 'NOT be in the URL path' — so a future session that reaches for the path form hits a failing test, not a blank page.

ITEM 3 — failure classes. classify() splits DataProviderError into missing_api_key / unauthorized (401,403) / rate_limited (429 or RateLimited) / transport / decode / upstream. Each logs one line naming the class, the consecutive-failure count, when the next attempt is, the underlying error verbatim, and what to do about it. A 401 additionally logs once at error level. The transport advice says explicitly that a transport error is NOT the URL shape — that is the class the original report actually fell into.
ITEM 3 — refuses to start with an empty key. PricePoller::start() checks the key before spawning and logs one clear missing_api_key error instead of looping on doomed requests forever.

ITEM 3 — bounded backoff. backoff_for() doubles the normal cadence per consecutive failure and caps at 5 minutes, resetting on success (with a 'recovered after N failures' info line). Tested for growth, for the cap across 1000 failures at both cadences, and for no overflow panic at the tail.

ITEM 3 — probes/alchemy-prices-probe.sh reads the key from the Keychain (falling back to $ALCHEMY_KEY, then the legacy file), normalises a pasted endpoint URL the same way normalize_api_key does, and curls both URL shapes printing status codes and timings ONLY. The key is never printed and never reaches a command line visible in `ps` (the Authorization header goes in via `curl --config -`). It then reads the result out loud, including the case where both return 000, which is the transport failure that was actually reported.

BONUS — envelope/audit.rs now creates its JSONL files 0600 as well. It holds no key material, but it does hold the user's addresses and transaction values, and it was the last file this app created under the umask.

Scope respected: nothing under src/ or tools/ was touched, no existing Tauri command name or parameter changed, no Seaport fulfillment and no real sniping execution — sniping is still simulated. The placeholder icons were left alone.
open_questions: Nonce serialisation is per-process. If the same private key is used simultaneously from another wallet client (MetaMask, Rabby, a script), a truly concurrent send can still collide — max(cached, chain_pending) recovers on the NEXT allocate, but it cannot prevent a simultaneous one. Fully solving that needs a nonce reservation the node participates in, which is out of scope. Worth a line in the UI if Emir expects to use these keys elsewhere.

check_transaction is now a documented footgun rather than a fixed one, as instructed (its behaviour and signature are untouched because the webview may call it). Once the frontend has moved its pre-flight to preview_transaction, consider whether check_transaction should be renamed to something that says it consumes — authorize_transaction — with the old name kept as a deprecated alias for one release. That is a coordinated frontend+backend change, so I did not start it.

preview_transaction reports the envelope's verdict only. It does not check the wallet's actual ETH balance or whether gas is affordable, so a preview can say authorized and the send still fail with 'insufficient funds'. Adding a balance/gas check would need an RPC call and an api_key parameter, which would make the preview no longer free to call on every keystroke. Say the word if you want a second, heavier preview_transaction_with_balance.

STATUS.md is NOT present in this working copy (only FINISH-BRIEF.md, README.md, FAZ1-DEMO.md, MANIFEST.json, WESTRON-CLAUDE-MCP-BRIEF.md), so I could not correct its 'NEXT SESSION STARTS HERE' section in place. The correction currently lives in the price_poller module docs, in two assertions, and in the probe script header. Someone with the real STATUS.md should delete or annotate that hypothesis there too, or the next session will re-implement it.

Expired envelope + engaged kill switch: an expired envelope is dropped on load, which takes its kill_switch_active flag with it. That is still fail-closed (an absent envelope authorises nothing, and check_and_authorize returns NoScopeDefined), but it does mean the user can create a fresh envelope afterwards without explicitly releasing the switch. If the intent is 'a kill switch engaged at shutdown must block even a NEW envelope until explicitly released', that needs a separate persisted latch — say the word and it is a small change.

Keychain item accessibility was left at the security-framework default (no kSecAttrAccessible override, no access-control / Touch ID requirement). Worth deciding deliberately: requiring device unlock or biometrics for wallet_* items would be a real security upgrade, but it changes the UX of every signature and needs Emir's call.

The Keychain items are not scoped to a signed application identity, because the app is not signed or notarized yet (explicitly out of scope this round). Until it is, any process running as the user can read them with `security find-generic-password`. That is still strictly better than 0644 files, but it is not the end state — the code-signing work is what makes the Keychain ACL meaningful.

Migration runs once per process and records its outcome in memory only. If it leaves anything pending, the counters reset on the next launch and it retries — which is the behaviour you want — but there is no persistent record that a migration ever failed. If the UI should nag until pending reaches 0, that state needs to go on disk too.

Envelope and scheduler state are JSON, not SQLite. rusqlite is already in use for alerts/sniping (many rows, queried), whereas these are one record each that is read at startup and rewritten on change; JSON keeps the atomic-rename-with-0600 guarantee that matters here. Easy to move to SQLite if you would rather have exactly one persistence mechanism.
